reading.body:
Google v. Oracle, decided in 2021, is the most recent Supreme Court fair use decision favoring a technology defendant, holding that copying roughly 11,500 lines of a software interface so developers could reuse what they already knew was fair use.

It joins Sega and Kelly in the set of precedents cited across the broad 79-case defense pool in this collection, specifically for the proposition that copying to build a platform others can create on top of weighs toward fair use, extending an interoperability-style argument from software interfaces to AI training data. Its own stated limit is the narrowest of any precedent in this collection. The Court repeatedly said it was deciding a case about computer code specifically, a functional work, and explicitly disclaimed broader application, leaving plaintiffs and defendants to read that limit narrowly and broadly respectively.

The data does not say which reading, narrow or broad, any court has actually adopted in the citing cases, only that the disagreement over the limit itself is part of the litigation record.
